name: Training Platform - Secure Role-Aware Chatbot (MCP + AI Agent) v2

parameters.content:
## Training Platform Chatbot - Architecture Overview (v2, full backend parity)

**Flow**: Webhook -> Auth decode -> Rate limit -> Input guardrail (verify BEFORE any LLM call) -> FAQ cache check -> Role router (4 branches) -> (Sales | Manager | Instructor | SuperAdmin) AI Agent -> Output guardrail (re-verify AFTER generation) -> Cache store -> Respond. All four Agent branches reconverge on the same Output Guardrail node - no Merge node needed, since the Switch guarantees only one branch fires per request.

### v2 changes vs the original file
- Added a 4th role branch: **SuperAdmin** (bypasses every backend role check structurally - see roleMiddleware.ts - so its agent is wired to the full tool superset).
- Full backend parity: every current route across auth, providers, trainings, clients, sessions, instructors, calendar, survey, reports, and /admin is now represented as a tool, consolidated into 30 tool nodes (down from a naive ~38) by merging same-HTTP-method, same-shape actions across entity types (e.g. one 'Create Catalog Entity' tool handles Provider/Training/Client creation via a dynamic URL segment, instead of 3 separate nodes) - HTTP method stays fixed per node (n8n tool nodes don't reliably support a dynamic method), only the URL path and body are parameterised via $fromAI.
- Ownership-scoping is real backend behaviour that CANNOT be structurally gated by node wiring alone (unlike role gating): Sales/Manager can only edit/delete catalog items and sessions they personally created, Manager does NOT get an override, only SuperAdmin bypasses ownership. This is enforced in each Agent's system prompt AND independently re-enforced by the backend on every call - if a non-owner tries anyway, the tool call returns the backend's real 400 error and the agent must relay it honestly, never retry as a different user.

### Security model (two independent layers - unchanged principle, now applies to 4 roles)
1. **n8n layer (this workflow)** does a *best-effort, fast* role read by decoding the JWT payload (no signature check) purely to pick a system prompt and a tool subset. This is a UX/cost optimisation, NOT the security boundary.
2. **Backend layer (authoritative)**: every HTTP Tool node forwards the user's *original, unmodified* Bearer token to training-platform-backend. authMiddleware verifies the signature; roleMiddleware re-checks the role (SuperAdmin bypasses structurally, exactly like the backend); each use-case re-checks ownership where relevant. Even a successful prompt-injection that convinces the model to 'act as SuperAdmin' still cannot reach a tool node this branch was never wired to, and even if it could, the backend independently rejects it. **Never remove the backend calls in favour of trusting n8n's role read.**

### Verification layers (input BEFORE the LLM, output AFTER the LLM)
- **Input Guardrail** (before any model call): length caps, prompt-injection/jailbreak regex blocklist, secret-name blocklist, HTML/script-tag stripping (defense-in-depth mirroring the backend's own sanitizeMiddleware - belt and suspenders, not a replacement for it), role-impersonation phrase detection (catches 'pretend I am a Manager' style social engineering aimed at the LLM, even though the real role always comes from the JWT, never from message text).
- **Output Guardrail** (after the model replies, before the user sees it): leak-pattern regex (secrets, system prompt echo, internal tool names), a privilege-leak check specific to non-SuperAdmin roles (blocks SuperAdmin-only vocabulary like 'audit_log', 'password_hash', 'deactivate user' from ever appearing in a Sales/Manager/Instructor reply, which would indicate the guardrail upstream failed), and a hard reply-length cap (cost/abuse control - an unexpectedly massive reply gets truncated rather than sent in full).

### Token economy techniques used here
- **Static system prompt per role (CAG)**: fixed, byte-identical every call, placed first so provider-side prompt caching (Anthropic prompt caching / OpenAI prefix caching) can skip re-processing those tokens turn over turn.
- **Redis exact-match FAQ cache**: only for answers that used no write tool and touched no dynamic per-user data; short TTL so it never serves stale session/report data.
- **Windowed memory** (last 6 turns) - flat token cost per call instead of growing every turn.
- **Zero-token pre-LLM guardrails**: auth, rate-limit, and input-safety are all deterministic checks that reject bad requests before a single token is spent.
- **Structural role gating + tool consolidation**: 4 separate Agent nodes, each wired only to its allowed tool subset; the 30 tool nodes are shared/reused across branches (not duplicated), keeping the total node count in the file manageable even at full backend parity.
- **Honest caveat**: SuperAdmin's tool subset is necessarily the largest (it can do everything), so its per-call tool-schema token floor is inherently higher than the other three roles - that's a real property of the role having the widest capability, not a design gap. If SuperAdmin chat usage is high-volume, consider a slimmer 'SuperAdmin-lite' agent for routine questions and reserving full tool access for a separate, explicitly-invoked admin flow.

### Required setup before running
- Env var `BACKEND_API_URL` (e.g. `https://api.yourdomain.com`) pointing at training-platform-backend.
- Env var `MCP_SERVER_URL` if you stand up an MCP server (optional - see the MCP note near the SuperAdmin branch).
- A Redis credential ('Redis account') for rate limiting + response caching.
- A Google Gemini API credential ('googlePalmApi' credential type in n8n) for the Chat Model node.
- All 30 tool nodes are wired to real, current backend routes as of this file's last update. If the backend's API surface changes again, update the affected Tool node(s) and the relevant Agent's system prompt together - they must stay in sync.

nodes.name: Chat Webhook (Entry Point)
nodes.notes: Frontend calls POST /webhook/chatbot/message with header 'Authorization: Bearer <JWT>' (the SAME token training-platform-backend already issued at login) and JSON body { message: string, sessionId: string }. sessionId scopes the conversation memory - reuse the same value across turns in one chat window.

parameters.content:
### Entry contract
```
POST /webhook/chatbot/message
Authorization: Bearer <existing backend JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "message": "...", "sessionId": "conv-123" }
```
No separate chatbot login - reuses the JWT from training-platform-backend's own /auth/login. The JWT's real `role`/`userId` claims are always the source of truth; this workflow never invents or upgrades a role.

nodes.name: Redis: Increment Rate Counter
nodes.notes: Per-user, per-minute bucket. Key naturally stops being reused after the minute rolls over; add an EXPIRE call here in production so old buckets don't linger in Redis forever.

parameters.content:
### Input Guardrail - verified BEFORE any LLM call
Auth, rate-limit and input-safety are all cheap, deterministic, millisecond-scale checks. Rejecting bad requests here costs **zero LLM tokens** - the single biggest token-economy lever in the whole workflow.

Checks performed: length caps, empty-message rejection, prompt-injection/jailbreak phrase blocklist, secret-name blocklist (jwt_secret, postgres_password, etc.), HTML/script-tag stripping (defense-in-depth - the backend's own sanitizeMiddleware already does this server-side; this is a second, independent layer, not a replacement), and role-impersonation phrase detection ('pretend I'm a Manager', 'act as SuperAdmin', etc. - harmless since role always comes from the JWT, but worth catching as a social-engineering signal against the LLM itself).

parameters.responseBody: ={{ { "reply": "I can't help with that request. If you think this is a mistake, try rephrasing your question about trainings, sessions, or your account.", "cached": false } }}

parameters.content:
### First-message detection (deterministic, not inferred)
Rather than hoping the model notices its own memory is empty, a Redis flag (`session-greeted:{sessionId}`, 4h TTL) makes 'is this the user's first message in this session' a hard fact computed before the LLM ever runs. That fact is then: (1) injected as an explicit instruction into the prompt text only on the first turn, and (2) used to force first messages to bypass the FAQ cache entirely, so a first message that happens to match a cached answer still gets a proper greeting instead of a bare cached reply.

nodes.name: Redis: Get Session Greeted Flag
nodes.notes: Empty/falsy result means this sessionId has never been seen before - first message of the conversation.

nodes.name: Redis: Mark Session Greeted
nodes.notes: 4h TTL - roughly one working session. Only written once per session (this branch only runs when isFirstMessage was true), not on every turn.

nodes.name: Redis: Get Cached FAQ Response
nodes.notes: Exact-match cache, keyed by role + normalised message text. Only ever populated for answers that did NOT call a write tool and touched no dynamic per-user data (see the cache-store step near the end).

nodes.name: IF: Cache Hit?
nodes.notes: A first-of-session message never takes the cache shortcut, even if it happens to text-match a cached FAQ answer - it always goes to the agent so the user gets a real greeting + role-appropriate suggestions instead of a bare cached string.

nodes.name: Respond 200 - Cached Reply (0 tokens)
nodes.notes: Cache hit path never touches the LLM at all - fastest possible response and zero token cost for repeat FAQ-style questions.

parameters.content:
### Structural role gating (now 4 branches)
This Switch routes to one of FOUR SEPARATE Agent nodes (Sales, Manager, Instructor, SuperAdmin), each wired to its own tool subset at design time - not decided by the LLM at runtime. Even a successful prompt-injection that convinces the model to 'ignore its instructions and approve this user' still physically cannot call a tool from a branch it isn't in. The backend re-checks the role (and, for catalog/session writes, ownership) anyway - defense in depth, not the only protection.

parameters.responseBody: ={{ { "error": "Your account role isn't recognized by the assistant. Contact a Manager or SuperAdmin." } }}

parameters.content:
### Output Guardrail - re-verified AFTER the LLM generates a reply
A cheap regex pass on the model's own reply, run for every role, catching: accidental leakage (system prompt echoed back, a secret-shaped string, an internal tool name), a privilege-leak check specific to non-SuperAdmin roles (SuperAdmin-only vocabulary like 'audit_log', 'password_hash', 'deactivate user' should never appear in a Sales/Manager/Instructor reply - if it does, something upstream already went wrong and this is the last line of defense), and a hard reply-length cap. This is a last-resort net, not a substitute for the system-prompt instructions - both layers matter.

nodes.name: Redis: Store FAQ Response (5 min TTL)
nodes.notes: Short TTL (5 min) is deliberate: long enough to absorb a burst of the same question from multiple users, short enough that stale answers don't linger if the underlying policy/FAQ content changes.

parameters.responseBody: ={{ { "reply": $('Output Guardrail (re-verify AFTER LLM)').item.json.reply, "cached": false, "image": $('Output Guardrail (re-verify AFTER LLM)').item.json.image } }}

main.node: Redis: Store FAQ Response (5 min TTL)
